slides.body: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
The cause is named in the next section.

From video 125 you know what a pull request page computes: a commit list, which is everything reachable from the head and not from the base, and a diff, which is the three-dot comparison from the merge base to the head.
So when the page changes dramatically, one of three things moved: the head, the base, or the merge base between them.
In the lab the pull request is simulated as main..head and main...head, which is what GitHub computes.

slides.headline: The candidates
slides.body: The page shows a three-dot diff: either an endpoint or the merge base isn't what the author thinks.

slides.headline: The candidates
slides.body: Each has a local test. A rewritten main: the reflog of origin/main and the merge base.

slides.headline: The root cause here
slides.body: A topic branch, a branch for one piece of work, was aimed at main and updated from develop, an unreleased long-running branch.

slides.headline: Why "one small commit" felt true
slides.body: git log --first-parent shows the branch as Ravi experienced it: his commits and one merge.

slides.headline: The tempting fix, and why it is wrong
slides.body: git revert -m 1 of the merge commit, which adds a commit that undoes the merge: no forced push, and the diff shrinks.

slides.headline: The tempting fix, and why it is wrong
slides.body: And once this branch is merged, main contains those commits together with a commit that undoes them, so the later release of develop brings nothing: the re-merge problem.

slides.headline: The repair
slides.body: The branch has one author, so it's rebuilt: anchor the current tip, replay what came after the merge onto the merge's first parent, and publish with a lease, a forced push that's refused if the server's branch has moved.

slides.headline: GitHub, not Git: the approval
slides.body: Whether an approval survives a push depends on the rules: "dismiss stale pull request approvals" removes it when the diff changes.

slides.headline: Severity
slides.body: SEV 3. Nothing was merged. The near miss is the standing approval, not the file count.
Picture the pull request as the answer to one question: "what would arrive in the base if this were merged now?"
Ravi opened a door to develop to get one thing he wanted from it.
Where the picture breaks: you can close a door, and you can't un-open a merge by adding a commit.
For the method, one habit: read the commit list, not only the files.
Try it now. Thirty seconds, read-only.
A merge's subject usually names the branch that came in, as "Merge branch 'develop'" does here.

slides.body: To Ravi: GitHub showed what the branch contained, here is the reflog line, and the last commit has a new ID.

items: Blaming the platform or a rewritten main first. Root cause: the page is a computation over the head, the base and the merge base, and the reflogs showed that neither the base nor the head had been rewritten.
Updating a topic branch from a branch other than its base. Root cause: a merge makes every commit of the merged branch an ancestor of the result, so all of it enters the pull request.
Reverting the merge to shrink the diff. Root cause: the revert changes content and leaves ancestry, so the commit list stays long and a later merge of the same branch brings nothing.
Reading only the changed files. Root cause: the commit list, with authors, names the foreign commits directly; the file view only says that something is large.
Letting the old approval stand. Root cause: the approval was given to a different diff, and whether it is dismissed depends on a rule that may not be enabled.
